newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland plans army cuts as part of NATO bid.
newsitem.headline: Poland plans army cuts as part of NATO bid.

text.p: Poland's defence ministry has unveiled a radical plan to slash the size of the armed forces while making them more flexible and better equipped to function as a future member of NATO.

Under the plan, to be debated by the government before the end of May, the number of troops is to be cut by about a quarter to 180,000 in the next seven years, the armed forces chief of staff's spokesman Zdzislaw Czekierda said on Thursday.
"Funds generated by the cuts would be used to modernise our armed forces," Colonel Czekierda told Reuters, adding that it was too early to say how much would be saved by the downsizing.

The outline of the reform, presented to President Aleksander Kwasniewski by the forces chief and the defence minister on Wednesday, also provides for cutting the number of divisions, command centres and liquidating some garrisons.

The scheme should ensure the forces have at least as much of the right equipment they need to work with NATO from the moment Poland joins, said the defence ministry's development department director Boguslaw Smolski.

Poland, with the Czech Republic and Hungary, hopes to be invited to join NATO at its Madrid summit in July and enter the western military alliance in 1999, despite Russia's opposition to NATO's eastward expansion.
"Opponents (of Poland's NATO entry) should not be able to say that for NATO Poland is just new territory to defend," Smolski told Gazeta Wyborcza daily.

He said Poland, which now has 233,000 troops, 1,720 tanks and 440 combat aircraft, should first get equipment needed to adjust the forces to NATO's operational, command, communication and air space management procedures.
The government has also given priority to developing a new combat helicopter, the Huzar, which it hopes will become an export success, and to creating a new air defence system.

Poland needs about 100 multi-task fighters to replace its outmoded MIG 21 jets and effectively protect its air space, but Defence Minister Stanislaw Dobrzanski has said the first of them will not be bought for five years.

Some military analysts suggest Poland should significantly boost defence spending to upgrade its often outmoded Soviet-made equipment. But the government, faced with costly reforms of the social security and health care system, has been slow to allocate new funds for the armed forces.

In 1997, it plans to increase defence spending by 5.2 percent in real terms to 7.2 billion zlotys ($2.3 billion). But only 467 million zlotys ($151 million) will be earmarked for new equipment and 102 million ($33 million) for ammunition.
According to a U.S. administration report published in February, the expansion of NATO will cost more than $30 billion over the next 12 years for all involved.

New members selected at the Madrid summit should pick up 35 percent of the cost of joining, current members other than the United States would pay about 50 percent and the United States would pay 15 percent, the report said.
